words.intro: No German occasion is complete without a speech. A town’s 750th anniversary has seven of them, before anyone has eaten. Each begins by thanking the person before, and each is on time.

grammar[0].fact: German *Redemittel* are learned by the page before the C1 exam. They’re not exciting, but they do something useful: they buy time. While you say *In diesem Zusammenhang möchte ich darauf hinweisen*, you can decide what you’re about to say.

grammar[1].blocks[1].items[1].en: I look forward to your questions.
grammar[1].blocks[1].items[3].en: That brings me to the end.
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: No German audience has ever complained about a speech that ended before its time. They may not believe it, and they will thank you for it. Then they’ll head for the buffet.
grammar[1].fact: A *Festschrift* is a whole book written for an anniversary, of a person or a town. Many German towns have one for each round number. They’re rarely read, and they’re kept forever, in the cellar of the town hall, with the slides.

document.intro: A real invitation from a volunteer fire brigade in Austria. They were sixty years old and had a new fire engine, and they asked a vice-chancellor and a prince to come. Read the long phrase *zu der am Samstag … stattfindenden Feier*, and look at the word *Autospritze*.
document.fact: Volunteer fire brigades remain the heart of many small towns in Austria and Germany, with their own halls, festivals and speeches. A new engine is still blessed, and still a reason to invite everyone you can think of.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Say each one with a verb.
reading.intro: The town is 750 years old. It’s half past seven. There are 200 guests, one buffet behind a closed door, and a programme. Dr. Blum, who now chairs the town’s business club, is the seventh speaker. He has 34 slides. Frau Huber is in the front row, and she’s looking at the door.
reading.fact: Germans expect a *Festrede* to have facts, thanks and a structure, and to run long. Then there’s the *Grußwort*, the short greeting that opens any event. It’s usually read aloud on behalf of someone else who couldn’t come, and it’s very seldom short.
